introParagraph: If your Pennsylvania business has been denied or underpaid on a business interruption claim, state law gives you powerful tools to fight back. Pennsylvania's bad faith insurance statute, 42 Pa.C.S. § 8371, allows policyholders to recover interest, attorney fees, court costs, and even punitive damages when an insurer unreasonably denies, delays, or undervalues a claim. A well-drafted demand letter that cites the correct statutes and regulations often resolves disputes before litigation. This page explains how Pennsylvania law treats business interruption disputes, what deadlines apply, and how a properly structured demand letter can pressure your carrier to pay what your business is owed for lost income, extra expenses, and continuing operating costs.
lawExplanation:
Pennsylvania regulates insurance claim handling through both statute and the Unfair Insurance Practices Act (40 P.S. § 1171.1 et seq.) along with the Department of Insurance's regulations at 31 Pa. Code Chapter 146. Under those regulations, insurers must acknowledge claim communications within 10 working days, complete their investigation within 30 days of notice, and accept or deny the claim within 15 working days after receiving proof of loss. Failing to meet these timelines, or denying without a reasonable basis, can constitute bad faith.

The key weapon for Pennsylvania policyholders is 42 Pa.C.S. § 8371, the bad faith statute. To prove bad faith, the insured must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) the insurer lacked a reasonable basis for denying benefits, and (2) the insurer knew or recklessly disregarded that lack of a reasonable basis. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court confirmed in Rancosky v. Washington National Insurance Co. (2017) that ill will or self-interest is not required, only knowing or reckless disregard.

For business interruption coverage specifically, Pennsylvania courts interpret policies under standard contract principles. Ambiguous policy language is construed against the insurer (contra proferentem). Common disputes involve the meaning of 'direct physical loss or damage,' the period of restoration, calculation of lost net income and continuing expenses, and civil authority coverage. While many COVID-19 business interruption claims were rejected by Pennsylvania federal and state courts (e.g., Ungarean v. CNA), claims involving fire, water damage, vandalism, equipment breakdown, and supplier disruption remain viable. Successful claimants under § 8371 can recover interest at prime rate plus 3%, court costs, reasonable attorney fees, and punitive damages, which are uncapped and often exceed the underlying claim value.
letterStrategy:
A Pennsylvania business interruption demand letter should be specific, document-heavy, and explicitly invoke the statutes that expose the insurer to penalties. Start by identifying the policy, claim number, date of loss, and triggering event. Then itemize your damages with supporting documentation: profit-and-loss statements, tax returns, payroll records, utility bills, and a forensic accountant's calculation of lost net income plus continuing expenses during the period of restoration.

Next, cite the insurer's specific failures under 31 Pa. Code § 146.5 (acknowledgment), § 146.6 (investigation), and § 146.7 (acceptance or denial). If the carrier missed deadlines, ignored documentation, used a low-ball appraisal, or denied without explaining the policy basis, label each act and tie it to the regulation breached. Then invoke 42 Pa.C.S. § 8371 directly, putting the insurer on notice that continued unreasonable conduct will support a bad faith claim seeking interest at prime plus 3%, attorney fees, costs, and punitive damages.

Set a firm deadline, typically 30 days, for full payment or a written explanation supported by policy language. Reserve all rights, including rights under the Unfair Insurance Practices Act and the Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law where applicable. Send by certified mail, return receipt requested, and keep proof of delivery. A demand letter that quantifies exposure and signals litigation readiness frequently triggers a renewed adjuster review, mediation, or a substantially improved settlement offer before suit becomes necessary.
proceduralNotes: Pennsylvania's small claims (Magisterial District Court) limit is $12,000, which may cover smaller business interruption disputes; filing fees typically run $50-$150 depending on the amount. Larger claims are filed in the Court of Common Pleas, where filing fees vary by county (often $200-$400) and arbitration is mandatory for cases under $50,000 in most counties. The statute of limitations is four years for breach of contract (42 Pa.C.S. § 5525) and two years for bad faith claims under § 8371 (42 Pa.C.S. § 5524), so do not delay. Many policies also contain a contractual suit-limitation clause, sometimes as short as one or two years, which Pennsylvania courts generally enforce. Check your policy immediately.

faq.q: What damages can I recover for a bad faith business interruption denial in Pennsylvania?
faq.a: Under 42 Pa.C.S. § 8371, a court may award interest on the claim amount at the prime rate plus 3% from the date the claim was made, reasonable attorney fees, court costs, and punitive damages. Punitive damages are not capped by the statute and can substantially exceed the policy benefits when the insurer's conduct was particularly egregious. You can also recover the underlying contract damages, meaning the full lost income and extra expense benefits owed under the policy.

faq.q: How long does my insurer have to investigate my business interruption claim?
faq.a: Under 31 Pa. Code § 146.6, insurers must complete investigation of a claim within 30 days of notification, unless the investigation cannot reasonably be completed in that time. They must acknowledge communications within 10 working days (§ 146.5) and accept or deny the claim within 15 working days after receiving a proof of loss (§ 146.7). If more time is needed, the insurer must send written status updates every 45 days explaining the delay.

faq.q: Does my Pennsylvania policy cover COVID-19 business interruption losses?
faq.a: Most likely no. Pennsylvania state and federal courts have overwhelmingly held that COVID-19 closures do not cause 'direct physical loss or damage' required to trigger business interruption coverage, including in Ungarean v. CNA and similar appellate decisions. However, if your policy contains specific virus or communicable disease coverage, or you suffered a separate physical loss event, coverage may still apply. A careful policy review by counsel is essential before assuming denial is final.

faq.q: Can I file my business interruption dispute in small claims court?
faq.a: If your total damages are $12,000 or less, you can file in a Pennsylvania Magisterial District Court (small claims). However, most business interruption losses exceed this limit because they include lost profits plus continuing expenses over weeks or months. Larger claims must be filed in the Court of Common Pleas. Importantly, small claims courts cannot generally award the punitive damages and attorney fees available under § 8371 as effectively as Common Pleas can.

faq.q: What is the deadline to sue my insurer in Pennsylvania?
faq.a: Breach of contract claims have a four-year statute of limitations under 42 Pa.C.S. § 5525. Bad faith claims under § 8371 have a two-year limitation under § 5524. Critically, your policy likely contains a contractual suit-limitation clause that is shorter, often one or two years from the date of loss, and Pennsylvania courts routinely enforce these clauses. Read your policy carefully and calendar the earliest applicable deadline immediately to preserve your rights.
